title: Handheld 3D LiDAR scanner (in progress)
text:
Goal
Design a portable, self-contained 3D/2D scanner that measures a room and displays its geometry in real time. The fictional use case is an architecture firm or real estate agency that wants to survey a room quickly and generate a 2D floor plan and a 3D model.
The project covers the whole chain:

Electronics: custom PCB built around an STM32 microcontroller and the VL53L9CX LiDAR, from schematic capture to board bring-up.
Embedded software: C firmware to configure the sensors, acquire depth data in real time and manage communication.
Artificial intelligence: recognition of room elements (walls, doors, windows, obstacles), on the device or offloaded to the computer.
Application: data reception (USB, Bluetooth or Wi-Fi) and display of the 2D floor plan and 3D point cloud.
Mechanics: ergonomic enclosure designed in CAD and 3D-printed.

title: Handheld 3D LiDAR scanner (in progress)
text:
Constraints

STMicroelectronics components only.
Budget of about €150 for the whole project.
Battery-powered, with a low-power design.
Handheld device: lightweight and easy to use.

title: Handheld 3D LiDAR scanner (in progress)
text:
Approach
The team works in agile sprints and keeps a lab notebook (decisions, justifications, failure analysis). To limit risk, the priority is a minimum viable product: 2D mapping and raw LiDAR data transmission first, then AI and 3D rendering. Each sensor is validated on a Nucleo development board before the PCB is manufactured.

title: Handheld 3D LiDAR scanner (in progress)
text:
Progress
IMU validation. I brought up the STEVAL-MKI227KA evaluation board (LSM6DSV16X) on a NUCLEO-F410RB over I2C:

I2C bus scan and sensor identification through its WHO_AM_I register;
accelerometer and gyroscope configured at 30 Hz by reading and writing registers directly with the HAL;
acceleration, angular rate and temperature streamed over the serial port, with a wiring and troubleshooting guide for the team.

Next steps: VL53L9CX LiDAR integration, then PCB design.

title: Dungeon Explorer: 2D adventure game in Java
text:
The game
The player controls a hero in a top-down dungeon. The goal is to reach the exit portal while avoiding enemies and traps, some of which move.

Text-file levels: each character in a level.txt file maps to a tile (wall, rock, trap, portal…). New levels can be created without touching the code.
Lives: an animated heart bar loses one life on each contact with an enemy or a trap.
Sprint: holding Shift makes the hero run and drains a stamina bar, which refills as soon as they stop running.
Screens: title screen, game-over screen and victory screen with a “Play again” button, handled with a CardLayout.
Animations: the hero and enemies are animated from sprite sheets.

title: Dungeon Explorer: 2D adventure game in Java
text:
Architecture
The game runs on three independent engines, each driven by its own Swing Timer (every 50 ms):

RenderEngine draws every displayable object.
PhysicEngine handles movement and collisions: a SolidSprite blocks the way, a plain Sprite can be walked through.
GameEngine reads keyboard input and manages the game state (win, game over).

title: Dungeon Explorer: 2D adventure game in Java
text:
Object-oriented concepts applied

Interfaces: Displayable requires a draw method and Engine an update method, so the engines can process lists of objects without knowing their exact type.
Inheritance: Sprite holds a position and an image; SolidSprite adds a hitbox; DynamicSprite adds movement; EnemySprite and MovingTrapSprite specialise that movement.
Polymorphism: each sprite type overrides its drawing, for example to animate a sprite sheet.
Separation of concerns: rendering, physics and game logic evolve independently.

title: PC_BOT: autonomous mobile robot with wireless telemetry
text:
Goal
PC_BOT is a small wheeled robot designed to map a room. Several robots position themselves along the walls, move autonomously while avoiding obstacles and share their positions over radio. Each robot continuously sends its distances to obstacles, orientation, speed and acceleration to a base station, which builds a 2D map of the room.

title: PC_BOT: autonomous mobile robot with wireless telemetry
text:
Requirements







Function
Chosen solution




Autonomous motion
2 DC gear motors driven by PWM through a DRV8411A driver


Obstacle sensing
VL53L0X time-of-flight sensor (I2C)


Orientation and motion
LSM6DSOX inertial measurement unit (I2C)


Communication
nRF24L01+ 2.4 GHz radio module (SPI)


Power
18650 Li-ion battery (3400 mAh), BQ25896 charger over USB-C, 3.3 V regulator


Main controller
STM32G431KBT6 microcontroller

Hardware architecture

        TOF[VL53L0X ToF sensor]

    MCU -- "SDA / SCL" --- BUS_I2C
    MCU -- "MOSI / MISO / SCK" --- BUS_SPI
    MCU -- "PWM" --- DRV
    DRV --- M1

    USB -- "Charge" --- BQ
    BAT -- "Energy" --- BQ
    BQ -- "VCC" --- MCU

    NRF -. "2.4 GHz radio" .-> Station[Base station]






The sensors (ToF, IMU, charger) share an I2C bus with 4.7 kΩ pull-ups. The radio module sits on a faster, full-duplex SPI bus to stream data continuously. The STM32 is programmed and debugged through an ST-LINK (SWD) connector.

title: PC_BOT: autonomous mobile robot with wireless telemetry
text:
What I did
PCB design (KiCad). Full schematic and layout of a 4-layer SMD board: microcontroller, Li-ion charging chain (BQ25896 with its 1 µH inductor, USB-C connector), 3.3 V regulation, motor driver, sensor and radio connectors, status LEDs and buttons. Each component choice was checked against its datasheet.
C firmware (STM32CubeIDE). Before the final board was ready, each sensor was validated on an STM32 development board:

ToF sensor: distance readings over I2C. The sensor detects obstacles from about 3 cm to just under one metre, with a range that depends on ambient light.
Radio link: communication between two STM32 boards, each fitted with an nRF24L01+, in transmit and receive mode, with received frames displayed in PuTTY.

Assembly and bring-up. Soldering of the SMD components, then sensor-by-sensor testing on the final board.

title: PC_BOT: autonomous mobile robot with wireless telemetry
text:
Takeaways
PCB design was the longest and most rewarding part: going from a real specification to a manufactured board. The project also taught me that a single layout or soldering mistake can quickly cause a short circuit and damage the board and its sensors, which is why testing each block separately matters.

title: Background on the wave glider
text: Explanatory video on YouTube

title: Background on the wave glider
text:
Overview
Liquid Robotics is an American company specialising in autonomous marine robotics. It designs and builds the Wave Glider, an unmanned surface vehicle (USV) powered by solar and wave energy: it harvests the energy of ocean waves for propulsion. It can therefore spend several months at sea in a row, collecting and transmitting ocean data.
Its applications are mainly in defence, maritime surveillance, oil and gas, and scientific research, for example:

Monitoring of oil and gas infrastructure, of the atmosphere, and seismic and environmental monitoring
Defence (anti-submarine warfare, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance)
Maritime surveillance (detection of surface vessels for coastal and border security)
Scientific research (meteorological, climate and seismic data in the open ocean, ocean acidification, environmental monitoring, fish and ecosystem monitoring)

It carries batteries and atmospheric and oceanographic sensors, seismic sensors for earthquake and tsunami detection, as well as cameras and hydrophones for security, surveillance, research or protection of the marine environment.
Since 2007, Wave Gliders have been deployed from the Arctic to the Southern Ocean, for example to track great white sharks with researcher Barbara Block (Hopkins Marine Station), to patrol marine protected areas against illegal fishing for the UK Foreign & Commonwealth Office, and to assess the health of the Great Barrier Reef. They have also collected data during extreme storms and detected and tracked a diesel submarine during the Unmanned Warrior exercise in October 2016.

title: Background on the wave glider
text:
Design
The Wave Glider is made of two parts:

The float, roughly the size and shape of a large surfboard, which moves on the ocean surface;
The wing rack (glider), suspended below on a 4 to 8 metre tether, fitted with a rudder for steering and a thruster providing extra thrust in extreme conditions (turbulence, no current or strong current).

 
The wings can rotate within a range of about 60 degrees, so that their inclination always favours forward thrust on the float.
The Wave Glider exploits the difference in motion between the ocean surface and the calmer water below to create forward propulsion. More precisely, when the swell lifts and lowers the float, the glider rises and falls with it: the lift and drag acting on the wings then produce a force that always pulls the float forward.
No fuel is needed, which allows it to stay at sea for long periods.

title: Background on the wave glider
text:
Later developments
On 7 September 2017, Liquid Robotics announced a new-generation Wave Glider designed for very rough seas (sea state 6 and above) and cold, high-latitude waters, with a larger sensor payload and more energy and storage capacity for long maritime surveillance and environmental observation missions.

text:
At a glance







Context

Approach

Tools
Python (NumPy, Matplotlib), Tracker (video analysis), Kane’s equations, 4th-order Runge-Kutta

title: Research project: dynamic modelling of a wave glider
text:
Context
A wave glider is a surface drone that moves without fuel. It consists of a float on the surface, connected by a tether to a submerged glider fitted with pivoting wings. As the swell lifts and lowers the float, the glider’s wings turn this vertical motion into horizontal thrust. This lets it stay at sea for months on oceanographic, environmental or surveillance missions.
Research question: how can the float achieve optimal hydrodynamic motion without any external energy input, given many constraining parameters (component mass, float dimensions, tether length)?

title: Research project: dynamic modelling of a wave glider
text:
Objectives

Measure the prototype’s maximum speed under different wave conditions.
Find the tether length that maximises speed.
Numerically estimate the optimal glider-to-float mass ratio and the best angle of attack for the wings.

title: Research project: dynamic modelling of a wave glider
text:
Experiments
I built two prototypes. The first, tested in a bathtub with a crank-driven wave maker, validated the principle. The second (43 g glider, 153.5 g float) was tested in a wave tank with a motorised wave generator and foam to damp reflected waves.
The motion was filmed and analysed frame by frame with Tracker: for each run, I fitted the wave measured on the float with a sine function and computed the prototype’s average speed. I then compared three tether lengths (3.5 cm, 4.7 cm and 5.2 cm).

title: Research project: dynamic modelling of a wave glider
text:
Modelling

Forces: lift and drag on the wings, weight and buoyancy, drag on the float.
Kane’s equations: this method handles each body separately without bringing in constraint forces, which simplifies the derivation for a two-body system linked by a tether. It yields two coupled differential equations, on the tether angle and on the float’s horizontal speed.
Numerical solving: a 4th-order Runge-Kutta scheme written in Python, giving the float’s speed over time (simulated average speed of about 0.08 m/s).

title: Research project: dynamic modelling of a wave glider
text:
Results

Maximum speed reached for a wave height of about 2 cm.
Optimal tether length of about 5.2 cm for prototype no. 2.
Optimal mass ratio around 1.5 and optimal wing angle of attack between 20° and 30°.

Limitations and next steps. The model assumes the float follows the swell perfectly, a constant tether angle and planar motion. Possible improvements are an on-board sensor to measure the motion directly and an adjustable tether length.

title: Etch A Sketch on FPGA (VHDL)
text:
Goal
Build a digital version of the Etch A Sketch: two rotary knobs move a pen that draws on a screen. Here the knobs are two rotary encoders and the drawing is shown on the board’s HDMI output.
The project was built block by block, each time following the same method: schematic, VHDL, simulation, then test on the board.

title: Etch A Sketch on FPGA (VHDL)
text:
Architecture





flowchart LR
    ENC_G[Left encoder] --> DEC_X[Decoder X]
    ENC_D[Right encoder] --> DEC_Y[Decoder Y]
    DEC_X -- "pen x" --> A[Port A<br/>write]
    DEC_Y -- "pen y" --> A
    BTN[Left button] --> CLR[Clear logic]
    CLR --> A
    A --> RAM[(Dual-port memory<br/>720 × 480)]
    CTRL[HDMI controller] -- "pixel address" --> B[Port B<br/>read]
    B --> RAM
    RAM -- "colour" --> ADV[ADV7513 HDMI chip]
    CTRL -- "HS / VS / DE" --> ADV
    ADV --> SCREEN([Screen])

title: Etch A Sketch on FPGA (VHDL)
text:
1. Rotary encoders
A rotary encoder outputs two signals, A and B, shifted by a quarter period: the order in which they change gives the direction of rotation. The decoder detects edges on A and B and increments or decrements a counter of configurable width.

Synchronisation: A and B are not synchronised to the FPGA clock, so they go through two flip-flops before any edge detection, to avoid metastability.
Debouncing: on the board, a single notch sometimes moved the counter by several steps. The mechanical contacts bounce for a few milliseconds, and at 50 MHz each bounce looks like a real edge. A G_TICK_DIV generic subsamples A and B every 1 ms, which removes the bounce without missing any notch.
Validation: the counter is first wired to the 10 LEDs to read its value in binary on the board.




Edge detection and counter increment logic





Encoder simulation, clockwise then counter-clockwise rotation (Surfer)

title: Etch A Sketch on FPGA (VHDL)
text:
2. HDMI controller
The controller produces no colour: it scans the screen pixel by pixel and reports at each clock cycle where it is. It relies on two counters, a horizontal one (858 cycles per line) and a vertical one (525 lines per frame). The scanned area is larger than the 720×480 image: the invisible blanking areas are part of the standard and let the screen recognise the 480p mode.
A frame is 858 × 525 = 450,450 cycles, i.e. 16.7 ms at 27 MHz: 60 frames per second.



Horizontal sync: o_hdmi_hs pulse and r_h_active visible area over two lines





Zoom on the start of the visible area: the x coordinate starts at 0, with its one-cycle delay compensated


The frame memory is stored row by row: the address of pixel (x, y) is x + y × 720, from 0 to 345,599.



Generation of o_pixel_en and o_pixel_address over a full frame


To test the controller on the board, its counters are wired straight to the colours: red follows x and green follows y. On 8 bits the value wraps every 256 pixels, hence the tiles.



Gradient displayed in VLC from the board’s HDMI output

title: Etch A Sketch on FPGA (VHDL)
text:
3. Moving a pixel
A single white pixel is displayed at the encoders’ position. A register had to be added so that the colour arrives in the same cycle as the Data Enable signal, and the encoders were moved to the 27 MHz pixel clock so that the whole design runs on a single clock.

title: Etch A Sketch on FPGA (VHDL)
text:
4. Persistent drawing
For the pen to leave a trail, the image is stored in a dual-port memory with one cell per pixel:

port A writes white at the cursor position;
port B reads, in parallel, the cell of the pixel being scanned and directly gives the colour sent to the screen.

At 24 bits per pixel (about 8.3 Mbit), the image would not fit in the FPGA’s memory blocks (about 5.5 Mbit), so each cell uses 8 bits. The memory’s one-cycle read latency replaces the register of the previous step and keeps the image aligned.



LUT view of the design in Quartus: 219 ALUTs used for logic

title: Etch A Sketch on FPGA (VHDL)
text:
5. Clearing the screen
Pressing the left encoder’s button clears the screen. Since port B is reserved for display, clearing goes through port A, which then has two masters: the encoders in normal operation, and a counter that sweeps every address during clearing. A s_clearing signal selects between them by switching the address, data and write-enable together.
Clearing takes 345,600 / 27 MHz ≈ 12.8 ms, less than one frame, so it looks instantaneous. The pen stays where it is and drawing can resume immediately.

title: Etch A Sketch on FPGA (VHDL)
text:
Takeaways

Any signal coming from outside must go through flip-flops before being used.
A signal assigned in a process changes on the next clock edge, which explains the one-cycle offsets that must be compensated.
A passing simulation does not guarantee real-world behaviour: encoder bounce only showed up on the actual board.
